title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS) in older adults, with reference to chronic low back pain and fibromyalgia.
bps_function_set: conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper proposes a geroscience-informed BPS framework for geriatric MPS. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization), mentions psychological constructs (catastrophizing, fear-avoidance, depression), and minimally addresses social factors (social isolation, family support). Integration is directional between bio and psych, but triadic integration is partial.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that psychological factors (catastrophizing, anxiety, depression) directionally amplify central sensitization (bio-psych). Social factors are mentioned as outcomes or comorbidities but not mechanistically linked. Triadic integration is partial: the BPS definition includes bio and psych but omits social.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial framework but defines it as bio-psych only, omitting social
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological domain is elaborated with multiple mechanisms, while social domain is minimal and not integrated
conceptual_tensions_3: The BPS label is used as an organizing principle and intervention rationale, but triadic integration is partial
additional_observations_1: The paper introduces geroscience as a new lens for MPS, but this is primarily biological, not biopsychosocial
additional_observations_2: Digital therapeutics are presented as a way to scale psychological interventions, but social barriers (digital divide) are acknowledged
additional_observations_3: The case example illustrates real-world gaps in multidisciplinary care, but the framework remains largely theoretical
synthesis_note: This narrative review proposes a geroscience-informed BPS framework for geriatric MPS. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization) but treats psychological constructs as modulators without mechanistic depth. Social factors are minimally addressed. The BPS label is used as an organizing principle and intervention rationale, but triadic integration is partial: bio-psych integration is directional, while social is loosely attached. The paper contributes a geroscience lens but does not substantively operationalize the full BPS model.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and triadic integration is partial. Bio-dominant balance reflects the elaborated biological content. Integration is directional for bio-psych, mentioned for others.

title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS) in older adults; related chronic musculoskeletal pain and chronic low back pain.
context_note: Older adults in community, long-term care, primary/geriatric clinics, and Chinese/resource-limited settings; U.S. prevalence cited.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The model is operationalized as a clinician-facing review framework: age-specific pathophysiology, precision diagnostics, pharmacology/de-prescribing, non-pharmacological interventions, psychological therapies, and multidisciplinary care. It defines BPS pain as peripheral nociception, central processing, and psychological state, then maps interventions to those domains rather than testing a three-domain causal model.
integration_mechanism_summary: The strongest pathway is biological: aging-related tissue and inflammatory changes produce central sensitization, which psychological factors top-down modulate. Social factors mainly alter access to psychological care and multidisciplinary implementation; no full three-domain causal mechanism is specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: MPS is framed both as a localized myofascial condition with trigger points and as a complex geriatric syndrome rooted in aging biology
conceptual_tensions_2: The review advocates a geroscience-informed mechanistic cascade but states that interactions among aging mechanisms remain largely theoretical
conceptual_tensions_3: Digital therapeutics are promoted for access, while the digital divide is identified as a barrier to equitable uptake
conceptual_tensions_4: Multidisciplinary care is idealized, but the case example shows missing psychology and social work in China/resource-limited settings
conceptual_tensions_5: Non-pharmacological care is prioritized, but pharmacological precision prescribing and de-prescribing remain necessary
additional_observations_1: The review prioritizes high-quality evidence but uses a narrative thematic synthesis, not a pooled meta-analysis or formal systematic review
additional_observations_2: The social domain is mostly implementation/access: digital divide, family support, social determinants, and care-team composition
additional_observations_3: The clinical case is used rhetorically and illustratively, not analyzed as empirical data
additional_observations_4: Several citation placeholders are blank in the supplied text, so attribution is sometimes unresolvable
additional_observations_5: The framework is actionable for clinicians but not empirically validated as a model
synthesis_note: This narrative review operationalizes BPS as a clinician-facing multimodal framework for geriatric MPS. Biological geroscience mechanisms are the strongest thread; psychological constructs and therapies are integrated mechanistically with central sensitization; social factors enter mainly as access, support, and care-system gaps. It offers descriptive triadic integration but few tested cross-domain pathways.
coding_rationale: Biological and psychological content are elaborated; social content is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic, triadic integration descriptive. Typology true_integrative despite thin social domain.
biological_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, is a cornerstone of this decline. Beginning in the fourth decade of life, muscle mass decreases by approximately 8% per decade, accelerating after the age of 70. In MPS, sarcopenia creates a vulnerable substrate.
biological_factors_02_factor_verbatim: This leads to fascial stiffening, reduced tissue compliance, and impaired gliding between fascial layers. This increased stiffness can directly contribute to pain by compressing embedded nociceptors and small nerve fibers.
biological_factors_03_factor_verbatim: Underpinning these changes is profound mitochondrial dysfunction. Aging muscle is characterized by a decline in mitochondrial biogenesis, reduced efficiency of the electron transport chain, and an accumulation of mitochondrial DNA mutations.
biological_factors_04_factor_verbatim: Superimposed on these structural changes is a systemic, pro-inflammatory state known as “inflammaging.” This refers to the chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that characterizes the aging process.
biological_factors_05_factor_label: cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)
biological_factors_05_factor_verbatim: A key driver of inflammaging is cellular senescence—the accumulation of non-dividing but metabolically active cells that secrete a cocktail of inflammatory mediators, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
biological_factors_06_factor_verbatim: In many older adults with chronic MPS, the pain experience is no longer solely driven by the peripheral MTrP. The constant barrage of nociceptive signals from the dysfunctional muscle tissue leads to profound neuroplastic changes in the central nervous system (CNS), a process known as central sensitization.
biological_factors_07_factor_label: neuroendocrine dysregulation and the HPA axis
biological_factors_07_factor_verbatim: Age-related changes in the neuroendocrine system also play a crucial role. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, the body’s central stress response system, is common in older adults.
biological_factors_08_factor_verbatim: For instance, a high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency has been observed in patients with chronic MPS, with age and limited sun exposure being significant risk factors.
biological_factors_09_factor_verbatim: Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): While effective for acute inflammatory pain, the chronic use of NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) is strongly discouraged in the elderly.
biological_factors_10_factor_verbatim: Gabapentinoids (Gabapentin and Pregabalin): These drugs are widely prescribed for neuropathic pain, but their efficacy in nociceptive or mixed pain states like MPS is limited.
biological_factors_11_factor_verbatim: Selective Sodium Channel Blockers: A highly promising frontier is the development of selective inhibitors of the NaV1.8 sodium channel.
biological_factors_12_factor_verbatim: A pharmacological frontier with particular relevance to geriatric MPS is senolytic therapy—agents designed to selectively eliminate senescent cells that accumulate with aging and drive chronic inflammation through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).

title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome in older adults
context_note: International perspective with reference to Chinese healthcare system limitations
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS as an organizing principle to structure a geroscience-informed framework for geriatric MPS management, integrating biological aging mechanisms, psychological therapies, and social care coordination without specifying detailed cross-domain pathways.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that biological aging mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, cellular senescence) drive MPS pathophysiology, which is amplified by psychological factors (catastrophizing, anxiety, depression) through central sensitization. Social integration occurs through multidisciplinary team coordination, but explicit biological-social pathways are not specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between theoretical integration of aging mechanisms and practical clinical implementation
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between digital therapeutics promise and digital divide barriers for older adults
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between multidisciplinary care ideal and healthcare system limitations in resource-constrained settings
additional_observations_1: The review uses BPS as an organizing framework rather than an explanatory model with specified mechanisms
additional_observations_2: Biological domain is most elaborated with specific aging mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, senescence)
additional_observations_3: Psychological domain is well-developed with specific constructs and interventions (CBT, ACT)
additional_observations_4: Social domain is mentioned but lacks substantive development beyond team coordination
additional_observations_5: The review proposes a stepwise clinical implementation pathway suggesting practical application
synthesis_note: This narrative review operationalizes the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework for geriatric myofascial pain syndrome management. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization) and psychological constructs (catastrophizing, CBT, ACT) while mentioning social factors only in terms of multidisciplinary coordination. The integration is partial, with biological and psychological domains linked through central sensitization mechanisms, but social integration remains superficial. The review proposes practical implementation pathways but acknowledges evidence gaps for innovative approaches like digital therapeutics and senolytics in geriatric populations.
coding_rationale: BPS typology 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but social integration is minimal. Triadic integration 'partial' because bio-psych links exist but social domain is only mentioned. Domain balance 'psych-dominant' due to extensive psychological content and interventions.
